home.eyebrow: An educational digital experience from Jordan
home.intro: Discover the historic castle of Ajloun, known as Qal‘at al-Rabadh, through a virtual tour and a heritage library—then learn how to protect digital information and files, just as the castle guarded the region’s routes more than eight centuries ago.
home.heroArt: Illustration of a hilltop castle surrounded by a digital network
home.bridgeBody: The castle was built to watch over the roads and protect its surroundings. Today our digital memory—photos, documents and archives—needs similar protection: verifying file integrity, staying alert to deceptive links, and recognising fraud techniques.

tour.title: Virtual Tour of Ajloun Castle
tour.intro: Walk through eight stops that tell the story of Qal‘at al-Rabadh: its setting, its defences, its building phases and what it has lived through up to today.
help: Select any stop number on the plan, or use the “Previous stop” and “Next stop” buttons.
You can move between stops with the arrow keys when focus is inside the tour.
Each stop shows a badge indicating how well documented its information is and whether sources disagree.
The address bar keeps the current stop number, so you can share the link or refresh without losing your place.

approach.title: On the Summit of Jabal ‘Auf
approach.body: The castle stands on a high hill of Jabal ‘Auf near the city of Ajloun in northern Jordan, overlooking three major valleys that descend to the Jordan Valley: Wadi Kufranjah, Wadi Rajib and Wadi al-Yabis. This position allowed its defenders to watch over the routes linking southern Jordan with Greater Syria.
approach.fact: Local tradition traces the name “Ajloun” to a Christian monk of the Byzantine period, while “Qal‘at al-Rabadh” means the castle with a rabadh—the residential suburb that grew up around it.

moat.title: The Moat and the Bridge
moat.body: A dry, rock-cut moat surrounds the castle; according to some sources it is about 16 metres wide and 12–15 metres deep. Visitors cross it today on a bridge rebuilt by Jordan’s Department of Antiquities as part of its restoration work.
moat.fact: Sources differ on when the moat was cut: some include it in the original fortress, while others suggest it was dug during the 13th-century expansion.

gate.title: The Entrance and the Rising Passage
gate.body: Visitors enter from the eastern side and climb a long sloping passage to an older arched entrance decorated with carvings of birds, followed by the original gateway of the first fortress.
gate.fact: Winding entrances in castles were designed to slow attackers and expose them to the defenders. The sources we used do not document what the bird carvings signify, so we offer no interpretation.

core.title: The First Ayyubid Fortress
core.body: ‘Izz al-Din Usama, a commander in Saladin’s army, built the fortress on the ruins of an old monastery. The original fortress had four corner towers linked by curtain walls and a double gate. It was meant to check Crusader expansion and counter the Crusader castle of Belvoir (Kawkab al-Hawa), protect the iron mines of Ajloun, and secure control of the routes and local tribes.
core.fact: Most sources date its construction to 1184 CE, while one academic source places it between 1188 and 1192 CE.

aybak.title: Aybak’s Expansion
aybak.body: ‘Izz al-Din Aybak enlarged and refortified the castle for al-Mu‘azzam ‘Isa, the Ayyubid prince of Damascus. He added a new tower on the south-eastern side with a new entrance beside it, and raised the original building to match the height of the new tower. Most of the castle’s present form dates from this phase.
aybak.fact: Some sources describe Aybak as a “Mamluk governor” and others as the “lord of Salkhad”, so we give his name and role without settling on a single title.

halls.title: Halls and Galleries
halls.body: Inside, the castle is a maze of rooms, halls and galleries, which makes its architectural development hard to trace. One stone bears a carved cross, probably a remnant of the monastery that preceded the castle; excavations have uncovered traces of that monastery.
halls.fact: The castle houses a small museum display with artefacts from different periods.

signals.title: Beacons and Carrier Pigeons
signals.body: Some sources state that the castle was a link in a chain of fire-beacon sites and carrier-pigeon stations that relayed news across Greater Syria as far as Cairo. Today the same idea maps onto two cybersecurity concepts: data integrity and trustworthiness.
signals.fact: This information did not appear in every source we reviewed, so we present it as an account that needs further verification and give no figures for how fast messages travelled.

later.title: From the Mongols to Modern Times
later.body: The Mongols destroyed parts of the castle in 1260 CE, after which the Mamluk sultan al-Zahir Baybars restored it. In the Ottoman period a military garrison was stationed there, and when the Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt visited in 1812 he found about forty people living inside. Earthquakes in 1837 and 1927 caused heavy damage, and the Department of Antiquities later carried out restoration and consolidation work.
later.fact: An academic source notes that the Transjordan Department of Antiquities restored the castle between 1927 and 1929, and consolidation work is still ongoing.

name.title: The name “Qal‘at al-Rabadh”
name.summary: What does rabadh mean, and where does the name Ajloun come from?
name.body: “Qal‘at al-Rabadh” means the castle with a rabadh—a suburb or residential quarter that grows up around a fortress—referring to the settlement that developed around it. Local tradition attributes the name “Ajloun” to a Christian monk of the Byzantine period; this is a popular account for which we have no primary documentation.

usama.title: ‘Izz al-Din Usama
usama.summary: The commander who built the first fortress in the late 12th century.
usama.body: ‘Izz al-Din Usama was one of the commanders of Saladin’s army, and some sources describe him as a relative of Saladin. He built the fortress on the ruins of an old monastery to counter Crusader expansion and protect the routes and iron mines. Most sources date the construction to 1184 CE, while one academic source places it between 1188 and 1192 CE.

aybak.title: ‘Izz al-Din Aybak
aybak.summary: Author of the major expansion that gave the castle its present form.
aybak.body: In 1214–1215 CE, ‘Izz al-Din Aybak enlarged the castle for al-Mu‘azzam ‘Isa, the Ayyubid prince of Damascus, adding a new tower and entrance and raising the original building. Sources differ on his title, describing him either as a “Mamluk governor” or as the “lord of Salkhad”.

moat.title: The Dry Moat
moat.summary: A rock-cut line of defence surrounding the castle.
moat.body: A dry moat surrounds the castle; according to some sources it is about 16 metres wide and 12–15 metres deep. One academic source suggests it was cut during Aybak’s expansion, while other sources include it in the original fortress. Visitors cross it today on a rebuilt bridge.

towers.title: The Towers
towers.summary: Four corner towers in the first fortress, then a new tower in the 13th century.
towers.body: The first fortress consisted of four corner towers linked by walls, with a double gate. During the 1214–1215 CE expansion a new tower was added on the south-eastern side to protect the courtyards, and the original building was raised to match its height. Today the towers offer wide views over the surrounding valleys.

monastery.title: The Monastery Before the Castle
monastery.summary: Traces of an old monastery beneath the castle’s foundations.
monastery.body: Sources state that the castle was built on the site of an old monastery whose traces were uncovered during excavations. One stone inside the castle bears a carved cross, probably a remnant of that monastery.

ironMines.title: The Iron Mines of Ajloun
ironMines.summary: An economic and military resource the castle protected.
ironMines.body: Among the reasons sources give for building the castle is the protection of the iron mines in the Ajloun area, alongside countering the Crusader castle of Belvoir (Kawkab al-Hawa) and controlling the routes between southern Jordan and Greater Syria.

mongols.title: The Mongols and al-Zahir Baybars
mongols.summary: Destruction in 1260 CE, followed by Mamluk restoration.
mongols.body: In 1260 CE the Mongols destroyed parts of the castle, including its upper battlements. After the Battle of ‘Ayn Jalut, the Mamluk sultan al-Zahir Baybars restored the castle and cleared its moat.

burckhardt.title: Burckhardt’s Visit in 1812
burckhardt.summary: A Swiss traveller’s account of the castle in the 19th century.
burckhardt.body: The Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt visited the castle in 1812 and found about forty people living there. Earlier, during the Ottoman period, a military garrison had been stationed in the castle.

earthquakes.title: The Earthquakes of 1837 and 1927
earthquakes.summary: Two natural disasters that left a deep mark on the castle.
earthquakes.body: Two major earthquakes in 1837 and 1927 caused severe damage to the castle. An academic source notes that restoration took place between 1927 and 1929, and consolidation work continues to this day.

inscription.title: The South-West Tower Inscription
inscription.summary: An inscription referring to renovation work at the castle.
inscription.body: One source refers to an inscription in the south-western tower recording renovation work by ‘Izz al-Din Aybak. We were unable to consult the original text of the inscription or a documented image of it, so we do not show its text or a translation here until it can be verified from a primary source such as Jordan’s Department of Antiquities.

digitalArchive.title: How Do We Preserve Heritage Photos Digitally?
digitalArchive.summary: Simple steps to protect a digital archive from damage and tampering.
digitalArchive.body: Keep the original version of every photo unedited, compute its SHA-256 fingerprint and record it in a register with the file name and date. Store three copies on two different types of media, one of them off-site. Whenever the file is moved or downloaded later, recompute the fingerprint: if it matches, the file is intact; if it differs, its content has changed.

hash.title: File Verification with SHA-256
hash.intro: Make sure the file you have is exactly the original version—not damaged and not altered.
hash.whatBody: An algorithm that turns the content of any file into a fixed string of 64 characters called a “fingerprint” or “hash”. Changing even a single character produces a completely different fingerprint, while renaming the file does not affect it. That is why museums and archives publish fingerprints, so that anyone can check a file’s integrity.
steps: Choose a file or drag it onto the drop area, or switch to the “Text” tab to fingerprint some text.
Press “Compute fingerprint” and wait for the result.
Paste the trusted fingerprint published by the official source into the comparison field.
Press “Compare” to find out whether the file matches the original.
hash.dropTitle: Drag and drop a file here
hash.choose: Choose a file from your device
hash.privacy: The file is processed only inside your browser and is never uploaded to a server.

links.title: Suspicious Link Indicator Checker
links.intro: Paste a link to analyse its text and spot the common signs of phishing links—without opening the link.
how: Copy the link from the message without clicking it, then paste it into the field.
Press “Check link” to see the indicators and the suspicion score.
Read the explanation of each indicator, and when in doubt verify the sender through an official channel.
links.disclaimer: The tool analyses only the text of the link; it never opens or connects to it. The result is an educational estimate, not a final verdict: a harmful link can look clean, and a safe link may show some indicators.
links.analyzed: Analysed link (exactly as you entered it, unchanged)

summary.low: No serious indicators were found, but always confirm the sender before entering any information.
summary.medium: Some indicators call for caution. Do not enter sensitive information until you have verified the site through an official channel.
summary.high: Strong indicators of possible fraud were found. Do not open the link, and report it to the relevant team if it reached you in a message.

links.none: No clear suspicious indicators were found in the link text.
links.assumedScheme: The link had no protocol, so we assumed HTTP for analysis purposes only.
tips: Type the official website address yourself instead of clicking links in unexpected messages.
Be wary of messages that rush you or threaten to close your account.
Only enter your password on a site whose address you have verified.
Report any suspicious link to your support or IT team.

errors.invalid: The link could not be read. Please check that it is written correctly.
errors.tooLong: The link is too long to analyse (more than {max} characters).

dangerousScheme.title: Unusual or dangerous protocol
dangerousScheme.desc: The link starts with a protocol that can run code or open local content instead of a normal web page—a technique used in attacks.

noHttps.title: Unencrypted connection
noHttps.desc: The link does not use HTTPS, so data may travel unencrypted. This alone does not mean the site is harmful, but be careful before entering any information.

ipHost.title: Numeric address instead of a domain name
ipHost.desc: The link uses a raw numeric address instead of a known site name—rare on official sites and common on fraudulent pages.

atSymbol.title: An @ symbol before the domain
atSymbol.desc: This symbol can hide the real destination: the browser ignores what comes before it and goes to what comes after.

punycode.title: Domain encoded with international characters
punycode.desc: The domain contains a special encoding for international characters, which can be abused to imitate well-known sites with look-alike letters.

nonAscii.title: Look-alike characters in the domain
nonAscii.desc: The domain includes characters outside the basic Latin alphabet, possibly chosen to resemble the letters of a well-known site.

manySubdomains.title: Many subdomains
manySubdomains.desc: The link has many parts before the main domain, which can be used to make you think it belongs to a trusted organisation.

longUrl.title: Unusually long link
longUrl.desc: Very long links can hide the real destination or carry tracking and redirection data.

shortener.title: Link-shortening service
shortener.desc: A shortened link hides its final destination, so you cannot know the real site before opening it.

keywords.title: Enticing or sensitive keywords
keywords.desc: The link contains words usually associated with signing in, verification or prizes, which are common in phishing links.

hyphens.title: Many hyphens in the domain
hyphens.desc: Hyphens are common in domains designed to imitate well-known site names.

port.title: Unusual port
port.desc: The link specifies a non-standard connection port, which is uncommon for public websites.

executable.title: Link to an executable file
executable.desc: The link ends with a file extension that can run programs on your device, or with a double extension that hides the real file type.

encoded.title: Heavy character encoding
encoded.desc: The link contains many encoded characters, which can be used to hide its real content.

redirectParam.title: Redirect to another site
redirectParam.desc: The link contains a parameter that forwards you to a second address, which can be abused to jump from a trusted site to a fraudulent one.

brandLookalike.title: Possible imitation of a well-known brand
brandLookalike.desc: The domain contains a name resembling a well-known brand, but the main domain does not belong to it, or letters have been swapped for look-alike digits.

suspiciousTld.title: Frequently abused domain extension
suspiciousTld.desc: The link uses a domain extension that appears often in fraud campaigns, although many of its sites are legitimate.

awareness.title: Cybersecurity Awareness Center
awareness.intro: Essential skills for protecting your accounts and files—and the digital heritage archives held by cultural institutions.

phishing.title: Phishing
phishing.summary: Messages that impersonate a trusted party to steal your data.
tips: Check the sender’s full address, not just the display name.
Be wary of urgency, threats and offers that seem too good to be true.
Do not click suspicious links; check them first or go to the official site yourself.

passwords.title: Passwords
passwords.summary: A strong, unique password for every account.
tips: Use a long passphrase made of several words that you can remember.
Never reuse the same password on more than one site.
Use a trusted password manager to store them.

mfa.title: Multi-factor authentication
mfa.summary: An extra layer of protection even if your password is stolen.
tips: Turn on multi-factor authentication for your email and important accounts.
Prefer authenticator apps over text messages where possible.
Never share a verification code with anyone, even if they claim to be technical support.

updates.title: Security updates
updates.summary: Updates close the gaps that attackers exploit.
tips: Turn on automatic updates for your operating system and browser.
Download updates only from official sources.
Replace devices and software that no longer receive security support.

backup.title: Backups
backup.summary: The 3-2-1 rule protects data against loss.
tips: Keep three copies of important data.
Store them on two different types of storage media.
Keep at least one copy off-site, and test restoring it regularly.

social.title: Social engineering
social.summary: Tricking people instead of breaking into systems.
tips: Verify the identity of anyone asking for information or access, even if they seem familiar.
Never connect unknown storage devices to work computers.
Report any unusual request through official channels.

integrity.title: File integrity
integrity.summary: Make sure a file has not changed since it was published.
tips: Compare the file’s SHA-256 fingerprint with the one published by the official source.
Download files only from official websites.
Record the fingerprints of important archive files when you first store them.

heritage.title: Protecting digital heritage
heritage.summary: Digital photos and documents are part of our shared memory.
tips: Keep originals unedited and work on copies.
Document the source and usage rights of every image.
Limit editing permissions on the archive to authorised people only.

awareness.checklistIntro: Tick what you actually do. Your answers are not saved or sent anywhere.
checklist: I have turned on multi-factor authentication for my email.
I use a different password for every important account.

game.title: Save the Castle’s Heritage
game.subtitle: Twelve challenges in three stages
game.story: The digital archive of Qal‘at al-Rabadh has come under tampering and fraud attempts. You are the archive’s guardian: make your way through the gate and the walls up to the tower, and answer the challenges to protect the castle’s photos and documents.
rules: The game has 12 questions across three stages: the Gate, the Walls and the Tower.
You earn 10 points for each correct answer, up to a maximum of 120 points.
You start with three shields and lose one shield for every wrong answer.
You win by completing all the questions, and lose if you run out of shields.
You can switch the language at any time without losing your progress.
game.quitBody: You will lose your progress in this round and return to the start screen.
game.winBody: Your shields held to the end, and the castle’s digital archive is safe.
game.loseBody: The attackers got past your defences this time. Review the answers and try again.

q1.text: In which century CE was the first fortress of Qal‘at al-Rabadh built?
options: The 10th century CE
The 15th century CE
The 12th century CE
The 19th century CE
q1.explain: The fortress was built in the late 12th century CE: most sources date it to 1184 CE, and one academic source places it between 1188 and 1192 CE.

q2.text: Which commander built the first fortress?
options: ‘Izz al-Din Usama, a commander in Saladin’s army
The traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt
Sultan al-Zahir Baybars
Al-Mu‘azzam ‘Isa
q2.explain: It was built by ‘Izz al-Din Usama. Baybars restored the castle after 1260 CE, Burckhardt visited it in 1812, and it was expanded for al-Mu‘azzam ‘Isa in 1214–1215 CE.

q3.text: What was one of the main purposes of building the castle?
options: To serve as a summer palace for rulers
To check Crusader expansion and protect the routes and iron mines
To serve as a trading port
To serve as a public library
q3.explain: It was built to counter Crusader expansion and the castle of Belvoir (Kawkab al-Hawa), protect the iron mines of Ajloun, and control the routes between southern Jordan and Greater Syria.

q4.text: According to some sources, roughly how wide is the moat around the castle?
options: About 2 metres
About 50 metres
There is no moat around the castle
About 16 metres
q4.explain: According to some sources, the moat is about 16 metres wide and 12–15 metres deep.

q5.text: You receive a message saying: “Your castle archive account will be closed within an hour—click here and enter your password.” What should you do?
options: Click quickly so the account is not closed
Reply to the message with your password
Don’t click; verify through the official channel and report the message
Forward it to colleagues with the link to warn them
q5.explain: Urgency and requests for your password are classic signs of phishing. Go to the service yourself via its official address, and inform the support team.

q6.text: Which option gives the best protection for a digital library account?
options: A short password that is easy to remember
A long, unique passphrase with multi-factor authentication turned on
Using the same password on every site
Writing the password on a note next to the computer
q6.explain: A long, unique passphrase is hard to guess, and multi-factor authentication protects the account even if the password leaks.

q7.text: Which of the following links shows the most suspicious indicators?
options: https://www.example.org/library
https://museum.example.com/tour
https://example.net/about
http://192.168.10.5/verify-login.exe
q7.explain: The last link uses a numeric address instead of a domain name, has no encrypted connection, includes words suggesting sign-in and verification, and ends with an executable file.

q8.text: You find an unknown USB flash drive in the museum hall. What do you do?
options: Hand it to the IT team without plugging it into any device
Plug it into a work computer to find its owner
Plug it into your personal computer at home
Copy its files to the archive
q8.explain: Unknown storage devices may carry malware that runs automatically; leaving them for people to find is a well-known social-engineering technique.

q9.text: You computed the SHA-256 fingerprint of a heritage photo after downloading it and found it differs from the published fingerprint. What does this mean?
options: The image quality has improved
The file’s content has changed or been damaged, so it should not be trusted until verified
Only the file name has changed
It means nothing
q9.explain: Any change to a file’s content, however small, produces a completely different fingerprint, whereas renaming a file does not change it.

q10.text: What caused heavy damage to the castle in 1837 and 1927?
options: Floods
A major fire
Earthquakes
A volcanic eruption
q10.explain: Two major earthquakes struck the region in 1837 and 1927 and severely damaged the castle; restoration and consolidation work followed.

q11.text: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule mean?
options: Three copies of the data, on two different types of storage media, with one of them off-site
Three passwords, two numbers and one symbol
One copy is enough if it is recent
Deleting old files every three days
q11.explain: The 3-2-1 rule reduces the risk of losing data to a failure, theft or a disaster at a single location.

q12.text: An official alert from the museum computer’s operating system says a security update is available. What is best?
options: Always ignore it
Download the update from an unofficial site because it is faster
Turn off automatic updates
Install it as soon as possible from the official source
q12.explain: Security updates fix known vulnerabilities; postponing them or downloading them from unofficial sources puts devices at risk.

about.title: About the Project
about.intro: “Al-Rabadh Castle: A Digital Experience” is an educational project that links the heritage of Ajloun Castle in Jordan with cybersecurity skills, offering all of its content and tools in both Arabic and English.
about.mission: To present the castle’s history in an accurate, interactive way, and to draw practical lessons for protecting information and digital memory from its defensive role.
goals: Introduce the history and architecture of Qal‘at al-Rabadh in two languages.
Raise cybersecurity awareness in a simple and engaging way.
Provide practical tools for verifying files and checking links.
Encourage responsible digital preservation of cultural heritage.
Make the content accessible to Arab and international audiences on phones and computers.
about.identityNote: “Al-Rabadh” remains a historic name tied to Ajloun Castle in Jordan, and the project’s identity does not change when you switch languages.
accuracy: We rely on more than one source for each historical fact wherever possible.
A dedicated badge flags information on which sources disagree or that needs verification.
We never invent a translation or undocumented text; if no reliable translation exists, we say so.
For the latest official information, we recommend consulting Jordan’s Department of Antiquities.
about.sourcesIntro: The historical content draws on the following sources, reviewed in October 2026:

wiki.name: English Wikipedia — “Ajloun Castle”
wiki.note: Construction date, moat, expansion phases and earthquakes.

creighton.name: Creighton University — Introduction to the Ajlun Castle virtual tour
creighton.note: Academic source for the building phases, Aybak’s expansion and the 1927–1929 restoration.

roughguides.name: Rough Guides — Ajloun Castle
roughguides.note: Visitor route, bird carvings, Burckhardt’s visit and the beacon and carrier-pigeon account.

visitjordan.name: Jordan Tourism Board — Ajloun
visitjordan.note: Construction in 1184, expansion in 1214 and the castle’s role in protecting trade routes.

images: All illustrations, icons and the plan on this site are original vector graphics created specifically for the project and may be used for educational purposes with credit to the project.
The site does not use any third-party photographs.
The tour plan is approximate and illustrative, not an official architectural plan.
If real photos are added in future, they must be properly licensed (for example under Creative Commons) with the photographer, licence and source credited.
about.privacy: This site collects no personal data and uses no tracking cookies. Only your language preference is stored in your browser’s local storage, and files and links are processed inside your browser without being sent to any server.
about.helpIntro: A short guide to each section of the platform:

lang.title: Switching language
lang.body: Press the language button in the top bar and choose Arabic or English. The page direction changes automatically, you stay in the same section, and your choice is remembered for future visits.

tour.title: Virtual tour
tour.body: Pick a stop on the plan or move with the buttons and arrow keys. Each stop shows the documentation status of its information.

library.title: Digital library
library.body: Search for a word or filter entries by category, then press “Read more” to see details and sources.

hash.title: File verification
hash.body: Choose a file and compute its fingerprint, then paste the official fingerprint and press “Compare” to see the result.

links.title: Link checker
links.body: Paste the link without opening it and press “Check link” to see the indicators and what they mean.

awareness.title: Awareness center
awareness.body: Open each topic to see its tips, and use the checklist to assess your digital habits.
